outcome: The infinitude question is unchanged: no proof, disproof or claimed proof was found. Since 26 January 2024 three further primes of the form p_n# − 1 were found and logged (4778027# − 1 on 31 July 2024, 6354977# − 1 on 12 August 2024, and 6533299# − 1 with first public record 28 August 2024), each adding one term to the known list and none bearing on whether infinitely many exist. No AI system is named in any source for these.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many Kummer primes, i.e. infinitely many primes of the form p_n# − 1, where p_n# is the product of the first n primes (the primorial) and p_n# − 1 is the Kummer number of the second kind? Equivalently, are there infinitely many n such that p_n# − 1 is prime. The statement itself does not define 'Kummer prime'. The frozen page (line 580) links it to Euclid number#Generalization, whose status line asks 'Are there an infinite number of prime Kummer numbers?'. The other meaning of 'Kummer prime' is Kummer's regular prime (a prime not dividing the class number of Q(ζ_p)); that is a different bullet on the frozen page (line 590, 'Are there infinitely many regular primes ...') and is not what this bullet asks. Read this way the statement has no sub-parts beyond the infinitude question.

events.what_happened: Caldwell and Gallot tested p#±1 for all primes p below 100000, a computational check of the primality of both forms; cited in the Prime Pages glossary as [CG00] and in OEIS A006794 as Math. Comp. 71 (2001), 441–448 (the two sources give different years). Predates the frozen revision. The 'all p < 12000 in 2002' figure reported in a search summary of the Meštrović survey was not verified at source.

events.what_happened: George Lillie, 'About the Primality of Primorials', arXiv:2110.04302, submitted 10 October 2021. The abstract argues in the spirit of Mertens' theorem that the probability that p_n# − 1 or p_n# + 1 is prime is O(n^−1), gives O(n^−2) for both being prime, and reads this as evidence for three instances in which both are prime. It is a heuristic about probabilities, not a claim about infinitude. Predates the frozen revision.
events.revisions: One version (v1, 10 Oct 2021) per the arXiv listing.
events.delivers: A probabilistic heuristic on how often p_n# ± 1 is prime. It does not establish that infinitely many are prime, and the abstract itself calls the three-instance statement 'evidence'.
events.doubts: The abstract asserts 'We show' for the O(n^−1) bound and 'We provide proof' for a further claim; I read only the abstract and did not check the body, so the strength of those claims is unverified. No independent engagement was found.
events.direction: Heuristic evidence against a strong probabilistic reading of primorial primes being finite; it does not decide infinitude either way.

events.what_happened: OEIS A392860, added by Antti Karttunen on 25 January 2026: a(n) = 1 + Sum (p_i − 2)·(p_i#/p_i). Its comments describe the n-th Kummer number as the n-th primorial minus one, and give a limit comment credited to Amiram Eldar and Antti Karttunen. It concerns primorial-base expansions of Kummer numbers, not whether any are prime.
events.delivers: A sequence whose terms are built from Kummer numbers; does not bear on primality or infinitude of the Kummer primes.

events.what_happened: 'Almost all primes are partially regular' (arXiv:2602.05090, 21 authors, submitted 4 February 2026), announced on Axiom Math's blog on 5 February 2026. It proves that a density-one set of primes is partially regular in the sense of not dividing Bernoulli numerators B_2 through B_{2M(p)}. This concerns Kummer's regular primes and the Vandiver-type question, i.e. the other meaning of 'Kummer prime'. It is recorded here because it is the nearest 'Kummer prime' plus AI result I found, and it is a different problem.
events.revisions: One version (v1, 4 Feb 2026) per the arXiv listing.
events.delivers: For a density-one set of primes p, partial regularity in the stated sense (the even eigenspaces up to a bound M_α(p) vanish). It does not concern primes of the form p_n# − 1 and gives no information on whether infinitely many such primes exist. It is partial: it does not prove the full Kummer–Vandiver conjecture.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; the paper is about a different question.

summary: The bullet's link goes to the Euclid number article's Generalization section, whose status line reads 'It is not known whether there is an infinite number of prime Euclid numbers (primorial primes)' 'or prime Kummer numbers', with the open question 'Are there an infinite number of prime Kummer numbers?'. So 'Kummer prime' here means a prime p_n# − 1 (the Kummer numbers of second kind, OEIS A057588). The Wikipedia article was last edited 9 November 2025 and still lists the question as open. The minus-form primorial records are in OEIS A006794 (primes p with p# − 1 prime) and A057704 (the indices n), both last modified 11 October 2026, which means the OEIS list currently ends at 6533299 and records no newer term. Since 26 January 2024 the record shows three new terms: 4778027# − 1 (announced 31 July 2024, Kai Presler, Prime Pages submission 6 August 2024), 6354977# − 1 (announced 12 August 2024, Tom Greer, Prime Pages submission 17 August 2024), and 6533299# − 1 (Prime Pages submission 28 August 2024, credited to Christian Wallbaum, status 'Proven'). I could open the Prime Pages records and the OEIS pages directly, but the boinc-af.org PrimeGrid announcement pages did not load (DNS failure), so the announcement dates and finder credits for the first two come from search-engine titles and summaries; I did not find a PrimeGrid announcement for the third. The OEIS records on 16 December 2024 added the three terms to both sequences. None of the terms bears on the question. It asks whether infinitely many n have p_n# − 1 prime, and a further instance of a sequence that may be infinite moves that question not at all. The Prime Pages records for the first two list verification as 'External', since the site's own software ran out of memory; the third is 'Proven'. No human mathematician has publicly engaged with any of these records: they are computational records, and the only engagement is the database entries. I found no proof, disproof, partial result, or claimed proof of the infinitude question in any source, including arXiv (searched for 'p_n# − 1' and 'primorial' with 2024–2026 terms), OEIS, MathOverflow and viXra search results, and Erdős problems. The Booker–Simon paper (January 2026) does not address p_n# − 1. The Meštrović survey (arXiv 1202.3670, last revised July 2023) is reported in a search summary as stating that the infinitude of the p#+1 and p#−1 forms is unknown, but I could not read its text, so that statement is unverified here. The OEIS conjecture of Wesolowski (2016) that the prime before a prime p with p# − 1 prime exceeds p# − e·p is a gap conjecture, not a result on infinitude. Two close calls. First, the reading of 'Kummer prime': the frozen page separately lists Kummer's regular primes (line 590), and the 2026 Axiom paper 'Almost all primes are partially regular', with AxiomProver credited in its abstract, belongs to that other problem; I record it as a discounted event, and it is the one AI-credited result I found near the 'Kummer' name. Second, whether the three new terms are 'newly confirmed instances' that grow a set the bullet names: the bullet names the infinitude of the set, not its size, so I read them as neutral, but a later pass could read the growing known list as moving a quantity the statement names. Pre-window computational terms (up to 15877, plus 843301 in 2010, 1098133 in 2012, 3267113 in 2021) are recorded only as sources; the earlier discoveries are not individually itemized. No AI system is named in any source about these primes. The computing tools named (PRST, MultiSieve, PFGW, the Prime Pages software) are not AI. Other AI-prime headlines I met in search (a 2026 claimed bounded prime-gap result attributed to a model, and an Erdős unit distance result) concern other problems; I did not research them, and the model name 'GPT-6 Astra' in one of them could not be checked against any primary source.
competing_reading: The strongest reading for a later pass to weigh: the bullet's link is to the Euclid number article, so 'Kummer prime' means p_n# − 1, and each of the three 2024 finds is a new prime of that form, the first such primes known since 2021 and among the largest of the family. A pass that counts a 'newly confirmed instance' as moving the bullet's quantity would record 2024 as a year of progress. Against that: the question is whether infinitely many exist, and a finite addition does not change whether the set is infinite, as with Collatz verification to 2^71. A second reading treats 'Kummer prime' as Kummer's regular prime, which would make this record the wrong problem, and the Axiom paper the relevant event; I think the link settles the first reading, but I have not verified how the frozen page's authors intended the phrase.
what_would_settle_it: For the scope call: the Wikipedia list's definition of 'Kummer prime' in its own words (the link target is the Euclid number article; the list's source would confirm). For the events: the PrimeGrid official announcements for 4778027# − 1 and 6354977# − 1 (boinc-af.org or primegrid.com news), which would confirm the discovery dates and finder credit, and Prime Pages verification of the two 'External' records. For the infinitude question itself: a proof or disproof, or a result on the distribution of primes p_n# − 1 that yields infinitely many; none is known as of 11 October 2026 on the sources I could reach.
